rashi:a1.1: This applies only to an unblemished firstborn: [only it] is juxtaposed to the breast and thigh, since that verse speaks of an unblemished one, as is written just before it: “You shall sprinkle their blood.” But concerning a blemished one it is written, in the passage “Every firstborn” (Deuteronomy 15:22): “The impure and the pure alike.”
rashi:a1.2: A non-priest, who eats offerings of lesser sanctity: peace offerings, [animal] tithe and the Paschal offering.
rashi:a2.1: In the communal service: if there is no pure priest in that ancestral house [on duty], an impure one performs the communal service, as it is written “in its appointed time”: even on Shabbat and even in impurity.
rashi:a3.1: [The inference] speaks of a non-priest’s eating, and in eating a non-priest is superior to an impure [priest], as we said with offerings of lesser sanctity; for you cannot find any eating that is permitted to an impure priest and forbidden to a non-priest.
rashi:a5.1: And the other: the first tanna, according to Beit Hillel, would tell you: “gazelle and deer” are written three times in [the portion] “See, I [set before you]”: one for the statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Oshaya, and it has not been explained to us where [that statement is]. [Rashi, like the translation, reads a single statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Oshaya; the Aramaic printed on the daf reads two.]
rashi:a5.2: For the statement of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar: in Shechitat Ḥullin, in the second chapter (28a).
rashi:a7.1: Just as there: the breast and thigh, menstruating women may not [eat them], since an impure person who eats consecrated food is liable to karet.
rashi:a10.1: The Paschal offering that comes in impurity: when most of the community became impure through a corpse and they performed the Paschal offering in impurity, zavim and zavot may not eat of it, even though those impure through a corpse do eat it. Evidently we do distinguish between impurity that issues from his body and impurity that does not issue from his body.
rashi:a11.1: It is there: that zavim may not eat, because the Merciful One revealed explicitly that those impure through a corpse are permitted, and no others, as it is written (Numbers 9:10): “If any man shall be impure by reason of a dead body” etc. From it we infer: an individual is deferred to the second Pesaḥ, but not the community. So it was concerning one impure through a corpse that the Merciful One revealed “a man” and not the community, but the impurity of zavim stays as it was. But here, with a firstborn, the Merciful One wrote without qualification: “the impure and the pure.”
rashi:a12.1: One may not skin a firstborn from its feet: even a blemished one, stripping it by way of the legs with the whole hide intact, to make a bellows from it for smiths, or for sellers of honey and oil, who put [their wares] in sheepskins stripped whole.
rashi:a12.2: Nor disqualified consecrated animals: even though they were redeemed and he slaughtered them for eating.
rashi:a13.1: Which is not needed for him: on the Festival.
rashi:a13.2: It is Beit Shammai: who hold that a blemished firstborn remains in its sanctity, even after slaughter, like an unblemished one. And just as with an unblemished one one may not skin from the feet, because of the degradation of consecrated items, since it damages the meat (being wary of cutting the hide, he cuts the meat), so too with a blemished one one may not skin from the feet.
rashi:a14.1: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: who is stringent with disqualified consecrated animals, saying that even after slaughter they remain in their sanctity.
rashi:a14.2: Two sin offerings: which he set aside as a guarantee, so that if one is lost he will gain atonement with the other; and a blemish befell one of them.
rashi:a14.3: The unblemished one shall be sacrificed: as his sin offering.
rashi:a14.4: The blemished one shall be redeemed: and its money goes to the chests for voluntary offerings.
rashi:a15.1: The blemished one was slaughtered: after its redemption.
rashi:a15.2: If before the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled: it was slaughtered,
rashi:a15.3: Permitted: to be eaten, even though the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled before the meat of the blemished one was eaten, since we hold that once it came to be permitted through slaughter, the blemished one no longer has any sanctity.
rashi:a15.4: If after the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled: it was slaughtered, it is prohibited even for benefit, for it is a sin offering whose owners have achieved atonement, which is left to die; this is one of the five sin offerings that are left to die.
rashi:a16.1: Even meat in the pot … is prohibited: the meat of the blemished one, since he holds that even after slaughter they remain in their sanctity, and it is called a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement.
rashi:a17.1: Let him establish all of it in accordance with Beit Shammai: for it entered our mind that just as Beit Shammai are stringent with a firstborn, they are also stringent with other disqualified consecrated animals.
tosafot:a1.1: In brief: Tosafot note that the verse “and their flesh shall be yours” also speaks of a blemished firstborn: so it is for both Rav and the school of Rav at the beginning of chapter 4 (28a), for both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva at the end of Eizehu Mekoman (Zevaḥim 57a), and for both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili at the beginning of Beit Shammai (Zevaḥim 37a), who expound “their flesh” to mean both unblemished and blemished, or expound “shall be [yours]” to teach that a blemished firstborn is given to the priest. Even so, Beit Hillel’s a fortiori inference comes and removes [the blemished firstborn] from the juxtaposition, so that non-priests may eat it, since the juxtaposition “as the wave breast” can still be applied to the unblemished one. They cite parallels where an a fortiori inference overrides a juxtaposition or a verbal analogy: Zevaḥim 10b, on a guilt offering whose blood entered [the Sanctuary], although the Rabbis use the juxtaposition of sin offering to guilt offering for another matter; Kiddushin 14a, on the death of the yavam, and the rule that wherever indispensability is written no a fortiori inference is expounded; and the passage on positive time-bound mitzvot (“the little ones are obligated; women, all the more so”). The passage in chapter 9 (53b), where the juxtaposition of animal tithe to grain tithe (not tithing new for old) overrides the a fortiori inference from sheep and goats, is different: there the juxtaposition would be left without application if one followed the a fortiori inference, for although Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda needs it for other teachings (tithe taken by estimation and by thought; and gentiles’ consecrated items, Zevaḥim 45a), its main purpose is “year by year.” Nor is Ḥullin 116a, where meat in milk is permitted for benefit by a verbal analogy and prohibited even for benefit by an a fortiori inference, a difficulty for Kiddushin (56b), as they explained in Kiddushin. tosafot:a5.1: One for the statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak and Rabbi Oshaya: Rashi explained that it is not explained [where it is]. Rabbeinu Ḥananel explains that it is the one in the second chapter of Makkot (22a): one who mates an ox of disqualified consecrated animals [with another kind], or who drives an ox of disqualified consecrated animals [with another kind], is flogged; it is one body, and the verse made it two bodies. That is, the ox by itself is considered like a gazelle and a deer, which are two species; not as people usually explain there, that it is partly like consecrated items and partly like non-sacred. Rather it derives from “gazelle and deer,” as is said here.
tosafot:a7.1: One may not give it to menstruating women to eat: the same applies to one who had a seminal emission, for [Beit Shammai] permit only the impurity that was permitted with the Paschal offering, as is evident shortly.
tosafot:a14.1: As it is taught: He had before him two sin offerings, etc.: This baraita is in Temura, chapter Velad Ḥattat (24a), and it deals with one who set aside two sin offerings as a guarantee, and now one is unblemished and one blemished; while in the mishna [there: if the second was sacrificed] before the first was slaughtered, [the first] must die, since its owners have already achieved atonement. One may wonder: in the baraita the Rabbis prohibit the blemished one when it was slaughtered after the sprinkling of the unblemished one’s blood, yet in the mishna it is permitted; and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon prohibits it in every case in the baraita, yet in the mishna he permits it when it was slaughtered beforehand. My teacher says: the mishna deals with one who set aside a blemished animal and transferred [its sanctity] onto the unblemished one, so that all the sanctity of the blemished one entered the unblemished one, which took on its sanctity. Therefore, according to the Rabbis the blemished one is permitted in every case, since it is not like a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement, and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon distinguishes between where it was slaughtered before the sprinkling and after it. But here the case is that the unblemished one comes by virtue of its own sanctity, and he did not transfer the blemished one onto it but onto money, so it does not appear that its sanctity lapsed, since the unblemished one does not come by its power. Therefore, according to the Rabbis, if [the unblemished one’s] blood was sprinkled before the blemished one was slaughtered, the blemished one is prohibited, since it is like a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement; and according to Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon it is prohibited in every case, since it is like a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement.
gershom:a1.1: Eats of a firstborn: as it is written, “The impure and the pure shall eat it.”
gershom:a2.1: This can be refuted: what of an impure priest? It is reasonable that he eats of a firstborn, since he was permitted out of his general [prohibition] in the communal service, as it is written “in its appointed time”: even in impurity.
gershom:a3.1: We are speaking of eating: and as for eating offerings of lesser sanctity, a non-priest is better placed to eat them than an impure priest; therefore Beit Hillel permit. [And Rabbi Akiva:] just as with a gazelle and a deer one may feed a gentile together with him, so too with a firstborn.
gershom:a4.1: And the other: the first tanna holds that “gazelle and deer” is written three times: “Only with all the desire [of your soul]” etc. [Deuteronomy 12:15]; “Just as the gazelle and the deer are eaten” [12:22]; “Within your gates you shall eat it” [15:22]. One for the statement that Rabbi Yitzḥak said in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, and this statement of Rabbi Yitzḥak in the name of Rabbi Oshaya I cannot find in all of our Gemara. And one for the statement of Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, as it says in Shechitat Ḥullin: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says: What does the verse teach with “Just as the gazelle and the deer are eaten” etc.? It juxtaposes the gazelle and deer to a domesticated animal: just as a domesticated animal [requires] slaughter, so a gazelle and a deer [require] slaughter.
gershom:a5.1: To menstruating women: to priests’ wives who are menstruating, and a menstruating woman’s impurity issues upon her from her body. There, the Merciful One revealed “impure by reason of a dead body,” to exclude impurity that issues from his body.
gershom:a6.1: One may not skin from the feet: one may not strip an animal’s hide whole by way of the leg, for [use as] a bellows.
gershom:a7.1: An effort that is not needed: for the Festival. And not with a firstborn and with disqualified consecrated animals, because of degradation.
gershom:a8.1: Beit Shammai, who say one may not give it to menstruating women to eat: that is, just as they are stringent with it in this, so they are stringent in another matter too, that one may not skin it from its feet.
gershom:a9.1: One unblemished and one blemished: for example, where he set aside two sin offerings as a guarantee, so that if one is lost or a blemish befalls it, the second will be in its place.
gershom:a10.1: If after the blood of the unblemished one was sprinkled: the blemished one was slaughtered, it is prohibited, for it is a sin offering whose owners achieved atonement, which is left to die.
gershom:a11.1: Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon says: Even the meat of the blemished one in the pot: that is, even though it was slaughtered before [the unblemished one’s] blood was sprinkled, and even though the meat is in the pot, as good as cooked, since it was not eaten until after the sprinkling it is prohibited. And just as he is stringent here with this blemished one, which counts among disqualified consecrated animals, so he is stringent that one may not skin disqualified consecrated animals from their feet.
rashi:b2.1: And Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon: who is stringent with disqualified consecrated animals after slaughter: does he not hold what we learned, that they are sold in the butchers’ market? Evidently they do not remain in their sanctity, and because of this benefit to the Temple, since at times he will pay more when he redeems it at the outset, as we said, the Master permitted it. So too, let him permit skinning from the feet because of the benefit to the Temple: since he will sell the hide at a higher price, he will pay more when he redeems it at the outset.
rashi:b3.1: Damages the meat: so there is not that much benefit, because of the meat, since he cuts into the meat and strips it off with the hide.
rashi:b3.2: In the West they say: this refers back to above. That is, in fact it is everyone’s opinion that skinning from the feet is prohibited, since it is a great degradation, for he appears to be performing work with consecrated animals, as they sell the hide for a bellows while it is still on the consecrated animal.
rashi:b4.1: Lest he raise herds upon herds: that is, all agree that skinning from the feet is prohibited, for if you permit it to him he will come to delay slaughtering until he finds people who want whole hides, and meanwhile he will raise herds of disqualified consecrated animals and come to a stumbling with them in shearing and labor.
rashi:b5.1: Mishna. That was congested with blood: (Rashi adds an Old French gloss).
rashi:b5.2: Even if it will die: if they do not let its blood.
rashi:b5.3: One may not let its blood: even in a place where it does not make a blemish, where the wound can heal again. And so it is explained in the first chapter of Pesaḥim: since a person is anxious about his money, if you permit him in a place where it makes no blemish, he will come to do it in a place where it makes a blemish.
rashi:b5.4: He may let blood, provided that he does not cause a blemish: that he does not cut or damage its ear or the rim of its lip, which will not heal again. For the Rabbis hold: all the more so, if you do not permit him in a place where it makes no blemish, he will come to do it in a place of a blemish.
rashi:b5.5: He may not slaughter on its account: on account of this blemish, since he inflicted it, until another blemish befalls it.
rashi:b5.6: He may let blood even in a place where it makes a blemish: for Rabbi Shimon holds that an unintended act is permitted.
rashi:b7.1: Gemara. And the Rabbis say: he may let blood even in a place that makes a blemish: if he needs to let blood from that limb; he should not leave it to die.
rashi:b8.1: Vulnerable location: an exposed place, not guarded.
rashi:b9.1: Rabbi Yehoshua says, etc.: from now on it is not fit for eating, since perhaps it is impure, nor for sprinkling [as impure teruma may be used], since perhaps it is pure; and one may not destroy it. Therefore he exposes it so that it becomes impure and will be fit for sprinkling.
rashi:b10.1: Rabbi Meir: who forbids spoiling it and permits repairing it if he can do so without a blemish, saying he may let blood so that it will not die, holds like Rabbi Eliezer, who forbids causing it impurity and [says] he hides it so that it does not become impure.
rashi:b10.2: And the Rabbis: who permit inflicting a blemish before it dies, so that it will be fit for eating, hold like Rabbi Yehoshua, who says one may cause it impurity so that it will be fit for sprinkling. And Rabbi Yehuda, who says that even though it is dying and going to waste one should neither spoil it nor repair it, holds like Rabban Gamliel, who says one should neither repair it nor spoil it.
rashi:b11.1: As he acts by direct action: inflicting a blemish on it; therefore it should die on its own and he should not inflict a blemish on it.
rashi:b11.2: Indirect: merely, in that he places it in the vulnerable place and causes it impurity.
rashi:b11.3: He holds like Rabbi Yehoshua: who permits causing it impurity so that it will be fit for sprinkling, rather than leaving it fit for nothing.
rashi:b12.1: Only lest Elijah come: and say that no impurity touched it.
rashi:b15.1: All concede: the Rabbis too, even though they disagree about a firstborn congested with blood, [where] one who lets blood is inflicting a blemish on a blemished animal, for you have no blemished animal greater than this, since it will die [the printed text reads “is not inflicting”; the sense, as stated below, is that this is a blemish in a blemished animal]: all of them concede regarding meal offerings that one who leavens after one who leavens, for example, where one kneaded it with leaven and another baked it, both are liable, as it is written (Leviticus 6:10): “It shall not be baked with leaven,” and “shall not be made leavened” (Leviticus 2:11). And we expound in Menaḥot (55b): baking was included in “shall not be made leavened”; why was it singled out? Just as baking is distinct in being a single act and one is liable for it on its own, so too for every single act.
rashi:b16.1: One who castrates after one who castrates: even with a non-sacred animal; if one cut the testicles while they were still in the scrotum, and his fellow came, detached them from the scrotum and threw them away, both are liable.
rashi:b16.2: If one is liable for cutting: as is written after it, “and in your land you shall not do [this].”
rashi:b16.3: For detaching: detaching them and throwing them away, not all the more so?
rashi:b17.1: In a blemished animal: such as this firstborn congested with blood.
rashi:b17.2: “There shall be no blemish in it”: read it as “there shall be no [blemish put] in it,” that one may not inflict a blemish. And since it could have written “blemish” and wrote “any blemish,” it includes even a blemished animal, that one may not inflict another blemish in it.
rashi:b17.3: And the Rabbis hold: we expound the whole verse, “It shall be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no blemish in it,” which implies: [of] a perfect animal, fit to be accepted, I told you that you shall inflict no blemish in it, but not a blemished one. And Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Meir, but he decreed against a place where they make no blemish because of a place where they do make a blemish.
rashi:b18.1: From the outset: before he consecrated it, it had a blemish.
rashi:b20.1: Let them also be prohibited with blemishes: [prohibited] to inflict a blemish in it.
tosafot:b5.1: A firstborn that was congested with blood, etc.: [The printed Tosafot here consists only of the words:] one must look into what they disagree about.
tosafot:b16.1: To include one who detaches after one who cuts: Rashi explained that if one cut the testicles while they were still in the scrotum, and his fellow came, detached them from the scrotum and threw them away, both are liable. My teacher finds this difficult, for below in chapter Al Elu Mumin (39b) it implies that with detached and cut testicles they are still there: at the end of the Gemara on the outer threads that were damaged, where it says that detached and cut are not blemishes, since they are still there. And in that passage Rashi explained: detached, by hand, completely, but still hanging in the scrotum; cut, with a knife, still hanging in the scrotum and slightly attached; for cut is less than detached, as it says in our chapter above: “to include one who detaches after one who cuts.” End of quotation.
tosafot:b19.1: In brief: Tosafot ask why the Gemara calls an animal blemished from the outset obvious, “a mere palm tree”; let it say that the verse was needed for a firstborn, which has bodily sanctity and no redemption. They answer that the Gemara prefers to find a need that covers all consecrated animals. It could likewise have said the verse was needed for the present day, when one does not transgress the prohibition of causing a blemish even in an unblemished animal, and even according to the one who holds one liable for causing a blemish in a blemished animal, since nowadays it is worse, as stated in the first chapter of Avoda Zara (13b), being not fit even for its value; but the Gemara rightly finds a need that applies even in Temple times. And although they explained that nowadays it is worse than causing a blemish in a blemished animal, one should not wonder at our ruling below, that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon of the baraita, who permits causing a blemish in a blemished animal, while in Avoda Zara Rava forbade cutting off the hooves of consecrated animals nowadays because it looks like causing a blemish in consecrated animals: although causing a blemish in a blemished animal is permitted by Torah law, it is at least prohibited by rabbinic law, and here it was permitted only because of the bloodletting. gershom:b1.1: Which are strong enough to transfer [sanctity to] their redemption: since they are subject to redemption. But a firstborn’s sanctity is not so severe that it transfers to its redemption. So too, when one skins disqualified consecrated animals from their feet there is a benefit to the Temple, since the hide sells dearly for a bellows; let it be permitted to him.
gershom:b2.1: [ל״א, another version:] There is no benefit to the Temple, since what improves the hide damages the meat, for he cuts it and spoils it. Like one performing work with consecrated animals [an editor’s note: it seems it should read “since he prepares the hide for a bellows while it is still on the consecrated animal”]. Bellows.
gershom:b3.1: A decree, if you permit skinning from the feet: perhaps there are no smiths there who need them, and he will keep them alive until [such buyers] turn up there, and he will raise herds upon herds of them before the smiths come, and come to a stumbling with them in shearing and labor.
gershom:b4.1: Even if it will die, one may not let its blood: for if you permit him in a place where it causes no blemish, perhaps he will let blood even in a place where it causes a blemish.
gershom:b5.1: If he caused a blemish in it, he may not slaughter on its account: for we penalize him.
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Shimon says: He may let blood even where he causes a blemish in it, since an unintended act is permitted.
gershom:b7.1: With regard to which uncertainty developed: a creeping animal was found beside it, and it is uncertain whether it touched it or did not touch it.
gershom:b8.1: A vulnerable location: an exposed place.
gershom:b9.1: He should place it in a concealed location: so that impurity will not touch it, for perhaps Elijah will come and declare it pure.
gershom:b10.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds that since it is uncertain, one may cause it to become impure: [so as] to burn it under his cooking.
gershom:b11.1: He should do nothing new with it: he should not move it from its place.
gershom:b12.1: Rabbi Meir says here that one may not let its blood in a place that causes a blemish only because he acts by direct action.
gershom:b13.1: One who leavens after one who leavens: that is, one who bakes after one who leavens, for with baking the leavening is completed.
gershom:b14.1: And one who castrates after one who castrates: one who detaches after one who cuts.
gershom:b15.1: If one is liable for cutting: one who cuts the scrotum and leaves the testicles hanging; for detaching the testicles, not all the more so?
gershom:b16.1: For Rabbi Meir holds “There shall be no blemish in it”: whether unblemished or blemished, it is prohibited to make a blemish in it. And the Rabbis hold “It shall be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no blemish in it”: that is, in an unblemished one it is prohibited to inflict a blemish, but not in a blemished one. And this one congested with blood is like a blemished one.
gershom:b17.1: And the other: and Rabbi Meir, [uses] “It shall be perfect … there shall be no blemish in it” to exclude an animal blemished from the outset, from its mother’s womb, in which it is permitted to inflict a blemish, but not one congested with blood. [And as for] “let them also be prohibited to inflict blemishes in them,” it teaches us [with] “It shall be perfect to be accepted.”
gershom:b18.1: And the Rabbis: but it is written “There shall not be any blemish in it,” which implies: even in a blemished one, no.
gershom:b19.1: That is written for an indirect action: that there shall not be [a blemish] in it.
